summary: During Moses' absence the people ask for gods to lead them, and Aaron makes a gold calf that receives sacrifices at a proclaimed feast to Yahweh. Moses intercedes against the threatened destruction of the people, then breaks the tablets and destroys the calf; the Levites kill about three thousand at his command, and further intercession leaves punishment still unresolved.
whyItMatters: The covenant fails while its tablets and sanctuary instructions are being received. The chapter holds Moses' efforts to preserve the people beside the violence he orders, refusing a simple account in which either forgiveness or judgment removes the other.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: The camp below Sinai during Moses' prolonged mountain absence, followed by exchanges on the mountain and his return to the camp.
context.literaryForm: Covenant-crisis narrative with competing speeches, intercession, destruction of sacred objects, lethal judgment, and renewed pleading.

before.text: The sanctuary instructions have ended with skilled workers, Sabbath obligations, and stone tablets written by God. The narrative now reveals what the people have done during Moses' delay.

here.text: The scene moves between the calf below and intercession above, then between Moses' anger, Aaron's defense, the killings, and a further plea for forgiveness.

after.text: God orders the journey to continue but threatens not to accompany the people personally; Moses then presses for the divine presence to remain with them.

outline.heading: The calf and its feast
outline.note: Aaron collects gold, fashions a calf, and proclaims worship amid the people’s uncertainty about Moses.

outline.heading: Threatened destruction and Moses’ plea
outline.note: Moses appeals to God’s reputation and ancestral promise, and the announced destruction is withdrawn.

outline.heading: Tablets broken and the calf destroyed
outline.note: Moses descends, hears the celebration, and reacts to what he sees.

outline.heading: Aaron’s defense
outline.note: His account shifts responsibility and differs from the narrator’s description of his craftsmanship.

outline.heading: The Levites’ killing
outline.note: Moses orders violence in God’s name, and about three thousand people die.

outline.heading: Further intercession and continuing punishment
outline.note: Moses offers to be blotted out, but God names the sinners’ responsibility and strikes the people.

keyVerses.text: So Yahweh turned away from the evil which he said he would do to his people.
keyVerses.why: Moses’ intercession is followed by the withdrawal of the announced destruction.

keyVerses.text: The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses. About three thousand men fell of the people that day.
keyVerses.why: The account explicitly reports the large death toll resulting from the Levites’ obedience to Moses.

keyVerses.text: Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”
keyVerses.why: Moses puts his own place in God’s book into his plea for the people’s forgiveness.

questions.question: What do the people want when Moses delays?
questions.answer: They ask Aaron for gods to go before them because they do not know what has happened to Moses, whom they identify with their departure from Egypt. The request combines a perceived leadership vacuum with a new visible object of worship.

questions.question: Is the calf presented as entirely unrelated to Yahweh?
questions.answer: The people credit the calf with bringing them out of Egypt, while Aaron proclaims a feast to Yahweh before it. The calf’s worship therefore appropriates the story of rescue and the name of the God who rescued them.

questions.question: What does “stiff-necked” mean in God’s accusation?
questions.answer: It depicts a people resistant to direction, as a neck unwilling to turn. The charge follows the description of their rapid departure from what God commanded.

questions.question: What arguments does Moses make against destroying the people?
questions.answer: He calls them God's own rescued people, warns how Egypt would interpret their destruction, and recalls the sworn promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. The narrative then says God turns away from the announced disaster, presenting the appeal as consequential.

questions.question: What happens to the tablets and the calf?
questions.answer: Moses breaks the divine tablets at the mountain's foot, burns and grinds the calf, scatters it on water, and makes the Israelites drink it. The destruction is physical and confrontational, bringing the broken covenant into the camp through actions as well as speech.

questions.question: Why is Aaron’s explanation unreliable within the story?
questions.answer: The narrator says Aaron fashions the gold with a tool and makes the calf, but Aaron later says he threw the gold into the fire and the calf came out. His retelling also emphasizes the people's evil, obscuring his own deliberate part already described.

questions.question: How does the chapter portray the killing by the Levites?
questions.answer: Moses presents the order as God's command to kill brothers, companions, and neighbors across the camp. About three thousand die, and Moses speaks of consecration and blessing afterward; the text gives no individualized trial or list of offenses for those killed, leaving a grave problem of collective religious violence.

questions.question: Does Moses’ intercession mean there are no further consequences?
questions.answer: No. He asks for forgiveness and offers to be blotted from God's book, but God answers that those who sinned will be blotted out and promises a future accounting. The chapter closes with God striking the people because of the calf, without giving a further death count.

glossary.def: The gold object Aaron makes and the people treat as their rescuer in the worship scene.
A figure for stubborn resistance to God’s direction.
Erase from God’s written book, the action Moses offers for himself and God applies to those who sin.
